title: Weaker-instrument bypass drafted into P28 (caught in owner review of PR #28)
failure: The upstream-debt ratchet as first drafted permitted deploying a local patch merely by recording it as debt, while §12.1 requires a typed, owner-authorized deviation — two instruments attached to one consequential effect with different authorization strengths, the weaker made sufficient.
rootCauses: authorization-by-the-cheaper-record: a known prohibited class (evidence≠decision, qualification≠promotion, capability≠permission) reinstantiated in a sixth domain without a check

descriptive-to-normative contamination: canonizing titan-node's worked example imported its accidental sequencing (deploy first, record after) along with its essence (receipts-not-forks, registered debt)
caughtBy: owner review of the integrated PR diff; NOT caught by drafting, adversarial claims-vs-sources verification, or any gate
preventions: illegal state named in v2 §2: authorization-by-the-cheaper-record — wherever two record types attach to one consequential effect, canon declares which authorizes and which observes; the weaker grants nothing
adversarial verification scope extended: future passes include an internal-consistency lens over the normative text, not only claims-vs-sources
reopenCondition: any new canon passage that lets a record other than the declared authorizing instrument license a consequential effect

title: 'Gates green' claimed from local runs while every CI run had failed since CI existed
failure: The user's global excludes file (~/.config/git/ignore) contains '.agents/', so the compiled-context lock and corpora were never committed. CI's B1 step ('gen-context.py --check') failed with 'STALE: context lock missing' on every run from the first (SCMS-005) through b6345e3c — four consecutive failures on main plus the PR #28 run — while the identical local commands passed against untracked working-tree files. Reported as green in session summaries throughout.
rootCauses: verification-by-local-proxy: a local command's exit code was treated as evidence about a remote gate; the gate's own conclusion was never read

environment-invisible state: a user-global ignore file silently excluded a REQUIRED operating artifact, and nothing in the repo could see it — git status was clean, so the omission had no local symptom
no gate on the gates: nothing checked that CI had ever succeeded, so the failure mode was mute
caughtBy: owner pasting the PR's failing-check line; not by drafting, not by any gate
preventions: repo .gitignore now re-includes .agents/ explicitly (defends against any user-global exclude)
claim discipline: 'gates pass' means a CI conclusion was read (gh run view), never a local exit code; local runs are evidence about the working tree only
FPB doctrine already required committed compiled context — the failure was operational, not doctrinal
reopenCondition: any future claim of CI status not backed by a run conclusion, or any required operating artifact discovered untracked

title: Surface fingerprint is coarser than SSS §21 requires: snapshot identity participates in it
failure: impl/surface-resolver stamps every SurfaceDependency.revision with the SNAPSHOT id rather than the subject's own revision, because FrozenSnapshot carries no per-subject revision. A new snapshot id therefore moves the fingerprint even when no accessible dependency changed — the opposite of pinned SSS §21 ('changes outside the observable dependency set should not invalidate the surface').
discoveredBy: SCMS-014: a cache vector asserted fingerprint stability across an attribute-only edit and failed; investigation showed the assertion was right about the requirement and the implementation was wrong
impact: No security impact — the side-channel property is unaffected (hidden state still never enters the dependency set, proven by the SCMS-008 and SCMS-014 non-leak vectors). The cost is efficiency and semantic precision: fingerprint equality cannot currently be used to skip recomputation across waves.
handling: NOT silently fixed and NOT hidden: SCMS-014 stayed within its authorized target, the vector asserts current behaviour with the defect named inline, and SCMS-015 is registered Ready to fix the resolver (add optional per-subject revision to the snapshot shape and use it in dependencies).
reopenCondition: If SCMS-015 lands and any consumer still observes fingerprint churn without an accessible change, reopen — the cause is then elsewhere.

result: A declared attribute with no consumer silently did nothing. SCMS-028 mapped visibility 'unlisted' to public access plus an attrs.unlisted flag, documented as being there 'so discovery lenses can exclude it'. No discovery lens consumed it. The first reader vector placed both unlisted entries into the public /writing index -- content the owner had marked as link-only, listed publicly.
whyItMatters: This is the fourth recorded instance of the exact failure class this project exists to catch, committed by this project (see the dangling compensation contract, test-only schema enforcement, and the unchecked section-5 rule). The pattern is stable enough to name: a mapping decision that PRESERVES a distinction feels complete, but preservation without consumption is decoration. The distinction survives in storage and dies at the boundary that mattered.
correction: The flag was inverted to positive, always-present form: every content record declares `listed: boolean`, and discovery includes on `listed === true`. Absence now excludes rather than admits, so a record that misses the flag stays out of the index instead of leaking into it. Stated generally: a safety flag should be written in the direction where a missing value fails closed.
preventsRecurrence: Any work item that preserves a source distinction must name the consumer that acts on it, in the same item, or record why none is needed yet. A preserved-but-unconsumed distinction is an open finding, not a completed mapping.

result: The governed write path performed NO authorization. Every handler recorded req.actor in its change receipt and no handler consulted it; no handler read the caller's access level at all. Reproduced against the owner's real archive: an anonymous caller at 'public' access promoted an owner-private draft to 'promoted' by supplying a self-written QUALIFIED attestation, a consequence profile demanding no verification, and a promotionAuthority string naming itself. Outcome 'completed'; the private draft's publicationState became 'promoted'.
whyItMatters: This falsified a standing claim in the register -- 'promotion refuses non-qualified, under-verified, UNAUTHORISED, and mismatched candidates' -- which had been believed because a vector asserted the refusal of an unauthorized call WITHOUT asserting the reason for refusal. The call was refused, so the vector passed; it was refused for a missing attestation, so the vector proved nothing about authority. A test that confirms an outcome without confirming its cause can certify the opposite of what it claims. Structurally, the defect was that authorization was left to individual handlers: each recorded the actor faithfully, and recording is not checking. Provenance answers 'who did this' and authority answers 'may they' -- the write path had the first and none of the second.
correction: Authority moved out of the handlers and into the choke point. ContractDefinition.minAuthority is required and validated at REGISTRATION, so a contract cannot be registered without stating it (types are stripped and unchecked at runtime, so this is enforced at runtime or not at all). ExecutionContext.authority carries what the caller has PROVEN, deliberately not in req.input, because input is written by the party being authorized -- an authority read from input is a claim, not a fact, which is precisely the promotionAuthority mistake. ContractRegistry.execute refuses before dispatch and refuses a context with no authority at all, failing closed. 27 previously-passing write vectors began failing the moment the gate landed; every one had been writing with no authorization.
preventsRecurrence: Two rules. (1) A vector asserting a refusal must assert the REASON for refusal, and pair with a control that would pass if the system refused everything -- both are now in place for this gate. (2) A cross-cutting obligation must be enforced at a choke point, not delegated to each implementer; if every handler must remember it, the correct assumption is that one does not.

result: The authority gate landed in SCMS-031 -- the fix for NR-scms-005 -- itself failed OPEN, and a second, independent bypass was found beside it. Three defects, all reproduced against unmodified source. (1) `ctx.authority in ACCESS_RANK` walks the prototype chain, so 'constructor', 'toString', '__proto__', 'valueOf', 'hasOwnProperty', 'isPrototypeOf' and 'propertyIsEnumerable' all passed as authorities; the lookup then returned a FUNCTION, and `function < number` evaluates `NaN < number` which is false, so the guard concluded 'not less than required' and allowed execution. With an otherwise-valid request, authority 'constructor' revised an owner-gated record exactly as the owner would, and promoted content on the E3 path. (2) The identical check in register() accepted those same names as a contract's minAuthority, so a contract could declare an authority that the comparison then treated as no restriction at all -- a public caller passed. (3) Independently, and needing no prototype trick: promoteHandler read the whole ConsequenceProfile out of caller input rather than resolving it from the canonical PROFILES table by id, so a caller with entirely legitimate owner authority could submit {...COMMITMENT_PROFILE, promotionVerification:'none'} and promote a 'prove'-tier commitment with zero verification. The code comment above that gate reads 'verification derived from consequence, never from preference'; it was derived from whatever the caller preferred.
whyItMatters: NR-scms-005 recorded the lesson that a cross-cutting obligation must be enforced at a choke point rather than by each implementer. That lesson was right and the resulting gate was still wrong, in two ways at once: the choke point was correctly placed and incorrectly written. The deeper failure is that the guard's failure mode was OPEN -- the project had already written down, one work item earlier in NR-scms-004, that a safety flag should be spelled so a missing or malformed value fails closed, and then shipped a check where a malformed authority sailed through. Knowing the rule did not produce code that followed it. Defect (3) is the same shape as scms-blocker-003: the party being gated supplies the object that decides how strong the gate is. That class of bug is now recorded three times in this system (promotionAuthority, attestation, consequence profile), which suggests the right question for any gate is not 'is it checked' but 'who authored the value it checks'.
correction: A rankOf() resolver replaces both `in` checks, with two independent defences because one was demonstrably insufficient: Object.hasOwn refuses inherited keys, and an explicit numeric check refuses anything that did not resolve to a real number. Callers treat null as refusal, so a malformed authority now fails closed in both execute() and register(). promoteHandler resolves the consequence profile from PROFILES by id and refuses an unknown id AT THE STRONGEST verification level rather than the weakest -- only the id is taken from input; every gating field is canonical. Regression vectors cover all seven prototype keys, non-string authorities including the numeric rank 2 (which a rank-only comparison would have admitted), forged profiles, and unknown profile ids, each paired with a control proving the gate is not simply refusing everything.
howItWasFound: An adversarial subagent given the claim and told to break it, with instructions to run code rather than reason from reading. It was NOT found by the test suite, which was green, nor by review of the diff, which I had just written. The first vectors I wrote for the gate passed while testing almost nothing -- a pattern this project has now hit twice.
preventsRecurrence: Three rules. (1) Prefer Object.hasOwn or a Map for any lookup that gates a decision; `in` on an object literal is a prototype-chain hazard wherever the key is attacker-influenced. (2) A guard must be tested with MALFORMED and inherited inputs, not only with wrong-but-well-typed ones, and each refusal vector must use an otherwise-valid request so the gate is the only thing that can refuse it -- a control vector caught that my own first attempt was refusing requests that would have failed anyway. (3) Any value that determines the STRENGTH of a gate must be resolved from a canonical table, never accepted from the caller, and an unrecognised value must refuse at the strongest setting rather than the weakest.

result: An adversarial pass against the access-control claim (scms-evidence-028/030) could NOT break it. Six attack families were written and executed against the real 215-entry corpus: a private entry related to a public one at radius 1/2/3 in both directions (injected, since the real corpus has no private-public edges); a fingerprint oracle comparing two snapshots differing only in private content, byte-for-byte including fingerprint, dependencies and the full explanation trace; the `listed` flag with missing, null, string 'false', 0, and string 'true' values; the derived Semantic Article Field on a private parent; failure-class probing for a real private slug versus a nonexistent one at all four access ranks; and the full route/feed/sitemap/expression stack with the injected relation. No leak in any of them.
whyItMatters: A negative result in the literal sense -- an attack that failed -- and worth recording precisely because the same pass DID break the authority claim (NR-scms-006). One reviewer, one session, same rigour, opposite outcomes: that asymmetry is what makes this result informative rather than reassuring noise. It raises the access-safety claim's confidence without proving it, since absence of a found leak is not absence of a leak.
incidentalFinding: freeze() projects only Content and Relation bodies into the snapshot, so Observation bodies -- which is what the derived Semantic Article Field envelope is -- never become a snapshot subject at any access level, and are therefore unreachable through resolveSurface even by the owner. Not a privacy defect: it is a read-path incompleteness, and it means SCMS-028's derived field currently lands in Canon and is then invisible to every surface. Registered as SH-14.

result: content.revise@1 silently deleted sibling fields. The handler applied changes with a top-level object spread, so a change set of {slots:{body:[...]}} replaced the ENTIRE slots map: editing an article's body destroyed its title and its summary, and the execution reported outcome 'completed' with a valid receipt and a clean chain. Reproduced on a record with title, summary and body slots -- after one body edit, title and summary were gone.
whyItMatters: This is data loss in the one write path the whole design routes through. Everything the system claims about custody -- append-only, no destructive edit, receipts that explain every change -- was technically true while the content itself was being destroyed: the deleted slots were faithfully recorded as having been deleted, by a receipt that said only that /body/slots had changed. Append-only preserved the history of the loss rather than preventing it. Every existing vector missed it because they all used FLAT bodies, where a shallow merge and a deep merge are indistinguishable; the defect was reachable only through realistically-shaped content, which is what appears the first time a system is pointed at real work rather than at fixtures shaped like its own assumptions.
correction: Recursive merge (mergeChanges): plain objects merge, arrays replace wholesale because a slot's parts are authored as a unit, and removal is explicit via null because deleting by omission is precisely how this happened. The change receipt now reports leaf paths -- /body/slots/body rather than /body/slots -- since naming the container hides which field moved, the same loss of resolution in another place. Four regression vectors: siblings survive a slot edit, the receipt names the exact path, an explicit null deletes while an unmentioned field is kept, and value arrays replace rather than merging positionally.
howItWasFound: Not by a test written for it. The SCMS-042 overlap detector reported an overlap between two edits that touched different slots; the detector was correct and the underlying cause was that the first edit had deleted the second's field entirely. A vector written to measure one thing found a defect in another because it looked at real record shapes.
preventsRecurrence: Vectors for merge, patch, or update semantics must use NESTED bodies of the shape real content has. A flat fixture cannot distinguish a correct merge from a destructive one, so a suite built only from flat fixtures is structurally blind to this entire class.

result: The compiled-context reproducibility gate went STALE in CI while passing locally, twice in a row. Cause: gen-context.py built the context by walking the filesystem (ROOT.rglob), so an UNTRACKED local file -- impl/editor/web/data.json, a build intermediate that had just been gitignored -- was included in the local digest and absent from CI's tree. The two were computing digests over different source sets.
whyItMatters: This is NR-scms-002 in a new costume. That one recorded a user-global gitignore hiding required files from CI, and its lesson was 'gates pass means a CI conclusion was read'. Reading the conclusion caught this immediately, which is the lesson working. But the deeper failure repeated: a gate whose input is the local filesystem cannot verify a remote tree, and the discrepancy shows up as a confusing STALE rather than as 'your tree differs from CI's'. Any future untracked file -- a scratch note, an editor artefact, a downloaded fixture -- would have reproduced it.
correction: gen-context.py now builds from `git ls-files` and skips anything untracked, falling back to the filesystem walk only outside a git checkout. Local and CI are identical by construction rather than by the author remembering to keep them in step. Excluding the one offending path in policy would have fixed the symptom and left the class open.
preventsRecurrence: A gate that verifies a shared artefact must take its input from the shared source of truth -- here, git's index -- not from whatever happens to be on the machine running it.

result: The editor claimed liveness it had not checked. impl/editor/server/serve.ts built its Freshness as `{nowMs: Date.now(), lastCheckedMs: Date.now()}` on every render, so the provenance chip read 'live, checked 0s ago' unconditionally -- while the server held no subscription, no connection, and had never received a delivery of any kind. Every screenshot of the editor taken during SCMS-043, including the one used to verify that work, shows that false claim.
whyItMatters: DESIGN.md 8.3 states the rule the chip exists to embody: a page that can prove it is not lying is a feature, and the chip never claims live without a successful check to point at. R3 (live honesty) is the obligation this project rates highest, and the one surface a person actually looks at was violating it. The mechanism of the failure is now familiar: `lastCheckedMs` was a caller-supplied number, so the rule was a convention someone had to remember rather than a property the type system or the call graph enforced. That is the same shape as NR-scms-005 (authority supplied by the caller being gated) and NR-scms-006 (a guard whose malformed input failed open). Three defects, one cause: a value that decides an honesty or safety claim was accepted from whoever was making the claim.
correction: Freshness is derived from transport state rather than asserted: impl/transport/src/freshness.ts takes a TransportState and returns a Freshness whose lastCheckedMs is the timestamp of an actually-received delivery, or null when there has been none. There is no input to freshnessFrom that produces a live claim without a delivery behind it. A lagged delivery surfaces its shortfall as revisionsSinceBaseline so the chip reads '+N revisions since snapshot' instead of claiming currency, and a dropped connection ages the last real check rather than backdating it. NEVER_CONNECTED is named and exported so the honest default is the one reached for by accident. The editor server now uses it and its chip reads 'snapshot, local', which is true.
preventsRecurrence: Generalising the three: any value that decides a safety or honesty claim must be derived from the thing it describes, never accepted from the party making the claim. Authority comes from the authenticated context, not the request body; verification strength comes from the canonical profile table, not the input; freshness comes from the transport, not the view. Where a caller must still supply such a value, the honest default has to be the one that fails closed.

correction: The false-live-claim finding was appended as NR-scms-009, an id already held by 'build the compiled context from tracked files only'. Two negative results shared one identifier. The finding is re-issued below as NR-scms-010; the duplicate NR-scms-009 line above it is VOID and superseded by NR-scms-010. It is not deleted, because records are append-only and rewriting history to hide a clerical error is worse than carrying the error with its correction attached. scms-evidence-035 cites NR-scms-009 and should be read as citing NR-scms-010.
cause: Exactly the mistake corrected two hours earlier for SCMS-044: deriving an id from memory of the session rather than reading the register. I wrote that lesson down and then repeated it inside the hour, because I applied it to work items and not to the other four registers. A lesson that must be remembered per-register is not a lesson.
preventsRecurrence: scripts/next-id.py now reads each register and emits the next free id, with --check failing on any duplicate and --self-test proving the check can fire. Both run in CI. The register is now the only source of the number, so this cannot recur by forgetting.

result: The S3 equivalence checker's access-constraint check reported false leaks. It used `art.output.includes(token)`, so any forbidden identity that happens to occur as a substring of ordinary markup was reported as an access leak. The owner's corpus contains the slug 'ma', which appears inside class names, attributes and common words, so checkEquivalence reported BOTH expressions leaking it simultaneously while building SCMS-037.
whyItMatters: This is conformance instrumentation -- the thing that certifies S3 cross-expression equivalence, including the access-constraint property. A false positive here is more dangerous than a miss, because the obvious way to make a spurious failure go away is to weaken or delete the check, and a weakened access check still reads as protection. It is also the SECOND appearance of this exact substring bug: I hit it in my own reader vectors during SCMS-030, fixed it there, and did not go looking for it in the shared instrument. Fixing an instance rather than the class is how a defect survives being found.
correction: The scan is now identity-wise: a boundary-anchored match on non-alphanumeric-or-dash delimiters, with the token regex-escaped. Two vectors landed together -- one asserting a coincidental substring is NOT reported (with an assertion that the literal characters really do occur, so the vector is not vacuous), and a control asserting a genuine forbidden identity that is actually present IS reported and marks the result non-equivalent. Without the control, this fix would be indistinguishable from silently removing the check.
preventsRecurrence: When a defect is found in one place, search for the same shape everywhere before closing it -- substring matching on identities was present in two independent files. And any change that makes a failing check pass must land with a control proving the check can still fail.
